issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is poorly matched to the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. 'People in uniform' more strongly suggests assault/police/military trauma than a pediatric medical crisis, and there are no accompanying medical or hospital-related cues to make this clinically coherent.

This creates a hard-to-explain mismatch with the trauma context and with the trigger items, which are hospital/illness-related.

vignette: When Kiet's son, Eli, was rushed into the pediatric ICU with a sudden cardiac arrest, Kiet's world fractured into the relentless beeping of monitors and the clinical chill of the ward. At forty-seven, after two decades of marriage to Chloe, he had spent three weeks standing at the glass partition, watching nurses adjust IV lines and physicians debate ventilator settings. The air hung heavy with antiseptic cleaner and the sharp, medicinal scent of rubbing alcohol used during emergency intubations. One afternoon, a junior resident's hasty assessment led to a critical delay in administering a vasopressor, and Eli's heart stopped for four minutes before they managed to restart it. When Eli finally stabilized, Kiet had come to believe that the medical team's negligence had cost his son precious time. He stopped sleeping through the night, his mind replaying the incident on a loop, cataloging every missed cue, every hurried note in the chart. Within months, the forest became his only refuge. As a park ranger in the northern reaches of the Pacific Northwest, Kiet traded sterile corridors for pine-canopy trails and quiet duty stations. Yet the illness did not stay behind him. During a solo patrol near a ranger station, the sharp tang of isopropyl alcohol in a donated first-aid kit made his knees buckle, a wave of dizziness washing over him until he had to sit against a trail register. The lightheadedness came without warning, a phantom echo of the ICU's dizzying shifts in altitude and urgency. He began to avoid his wife when she tried to bring up Eli's recovery, and he would leave the room the moment a fellow ranger began describing his own child's hospital stay. What frightened him most was the way others kept trying to pull him back into it. He stopped allowing anyone to mention the event, preemptively changing the subject or walking away whenever a colleague or relative brought up the trauma. His avoidance became a quiet habit, a way to starve the memories before they could surface. But the harder he pressed against the past, the more his mind turned to retaliation. He spent hours drafting letters he never sent, rehearsing accusations against the resident, and dwelling on what he would do to make the man feel the same helpless dread. That fixation became the engine of his daily suffering. Every time Kiet dwelled on what others had done to him and plotted revenge, his obsession actively lowered his threshold for environmental cues, dragging the hospital antiseptic scent and the phantom dizziness into the present. The rumination did not merely stay in his head; it functioned as a cognitive lens that turned routine ranger duties into a minefield of impending collapse. On a busy weekend, when a group of teenagers passed by with a cooler of beer, the alcohol fumes rolling off their jackets triggered a full-body flinch. Kiet was certain that the medical staff had been drinking to cope, that their incompetence was rooted in indulgence, and the obsessive blame only deepened the physiological storm. His dizziness returned in earnest, his vision tunneling as he stumbled off the trail, forcing him to abandon his shift early. The harder he ruminated on the assailant, the more violently the triggers responded, each flare of nausea or phantom scent reinforcing the conviction that he was walking through a world still trying to harm his son. The cycle cost him his partnership with the park district and strained his marriage beyond recognition. Chloe could not follow him into the woods where he refused to speak, nor could she navigate the sudden silences when a passing ambulance siren or a whiff of disinfectant from a nearby visitor's spray sent him into a cold sweat. He stopped taking calls from his supervisor, citing recurring dizziness and an inability to focus on navigation maps, though the truth was that his mind would not stop charting revenge. Finally, when Eli asked why his father never looked at him without searching for ghosts, Kiet realized the forest offered no sanctuary from his own mind. He booked an appointment with a trauma clinician, hoping for a way to quiet the relentless blame that had turned his own senses into traitors. What he most feared was that the man who nearly killed his son would never face consequences, and what he desperately hoped for was simply to sit in a room without feeling like his head was spinning, without smelling the ward, without having to plan a reckoning that would never end.
